source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1994) HTN Planning: Complexity and Expressivity
finding: Plan existence in HTN planning is only semi-decidable in general. It stays undecidable even with no variables, if a task network can hold two unordered non-primitive tasks.
numbers: Theorem 1: strictly semi-decidable even if propositional and all methods totally ordered (except the input network). Table 1 spans undecidable down to polynomial time.
quote: HTN planning is undecidable under even a very severe set of constraints.
limits: Pure theory. No human or LLM data. Worst case only; says nothing about typical domains.
agent_relevance: A method library with recursion and unordered subtasks can loop forever. O3 needs a depth or budget cap.

source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1994) HTN Planning: Complexity and Expressivity
finding: Decidability returns if you restrict either the non-primitive tasks or the ordering. Removing both restrictions together makes it undecidable.
numbers: Theorem 2: decidable if methods have a progressing form. Table 1: no non-primitive tasks gives NP-complete or polynomial; restricted cases range from PSPACE-hard and EXPTIME to EXPSPACE-complete.
limits: Table entries are for the paper operator model.
agent_relevance: Restricting what a method may produce (every method makes progress) is the cheap way to keep decomposition finite.

source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1994) HTN Planning: Complexity and Expressivity
finding: HTN planning is more expressive than STRIPS-style planning. The authors reject the view that HTN is only an efficiency hack.
numbers: Conclusion 1 of the abstract list. Restrictions on non-primitive tasks change complexity more than variables or total ordering do.
limits: Expressivity claim is contested; see next line. Theory only.
agent_relevance: Method knowledge adds real power, not just speed. A method library carries information that goal-only prompting lacks.

source: Wikipedia Talk: Hierarchical task network (cites Lekavy and Navrat critique)
finding: Editors argue the 1994 expressivity result is weak: HTN beats STRIPS only if the translation must be decidable, and the proof assumes infinitely many task labels.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Seen only as a search snippet. Editor discussion, not peer reviewed. Verify against Lekavy and Navrat before use.
agent_relevance: Treat HTN is strictly more expressive as a theory claim with caveats, not as evidence for LLM benefit.

source: Alford, Bercher, Aha (2015) Tight Bounds for HTN Planning
finding: Complexity of HTN planning depends on recursion, ordering and variables. Tight bounds range from PSPACE to 2-NEXPTIME and 2-EXPSPACE.
numbers: No recursion, total order, no variables: PSPACE. Acyclic with variables: NEXPTIME. Tail recursion total order no variables: PSPACE; with variables EXPSPACE. Arbitrary recursion total order no variables: EXPTIME; with variables 2-EXPTIME. Partial order tail recursion with variables: 2-EXPSPACE.
limits: Worst-case results for function-free first-order HTN. Confirms the 1994 semi-decidable result for the general case.
agent_relevance: Shallow hierarchies without recursion are the tractable regime. Keep method trees acyclic and shallow.

source: Alford, Bercher, Aha (2015) Tight Bounds for HTN Planning
finding: Allowing variables in methods raises worst-case cost by an exponential step; total ordering helps less than limiting recursion. This extends Erol 1994 finding 3.
numbers: Same table; e.g. acyclic partial-order without variables EXPSPACE vs with variables NEXPTIME (table rows as printed).
limits: Worst case.
agent_relevance: Prefer ordered steps in an LLM method library: ordering is cheap and keeps checking simple.

source: Munoz-Avila, Aha, Rizzo (2025) ChatHTN: Interleaving Approximate (LLM) and Symbolic HTN Planning
finding: A symbolic HTN planner asks ChatGPT for a decomposition only when no method applies. Verifier tasks check the effects, so any returned plan is provably sound.
numbers: Three domains (logistics, household robot, search and rescue), gpt-4-turbo, about 30 USD per domain. Full domain: 0 LLM calls, solved. Missing-method variants solved with 0 to 2 calls per task. Unsolvable problem: planner failed correctly. A no-verifier variant of the Full Domain was marked failed (X) after 3 to 4 calls in household and search and rescue.
quote: ChatHTN is provably sound; any plan it generates correctly achieves the input tasks.
limits: Tiny demos, no success-rate statistics. Soundness yes, completeness no (can loop). Without verifier tasks, LLM and handwritten methods interacted badly.
agent_relevance: Direct template for O3: use known methods first, call the model only for gaps, always verify the effect.

source: Munoz-Avila, Aha, Rizzo (2025) ChatHTN
finding: Even with well-crafted methods, extra methods can interact in unexpected ways and give plans that miss their effects. This is why verifiers were added.
numbers: Observed in the authors tests; reported as an analogue of earlier method-learning results (Hogg et al. 2008).
limits: Anecdotal, no counts.
agent_relevance: Check each subtask postcondition, not only the final answer.

source: Munoz-Avila, Aha, Rizzo (2025) ChatHTN
finding: If the task is unsolvable, ChatGPT still returns a sequence that looks like a plan. The verifier catches it.
numbers: Unsolvable tests: no solution output in all domains with verifiers.
limits: Soundness depends on the world model being checkable.
agent_relevance: Models will confabulate a decomposition for impossible tasks. Needs an explicit no-valid-decomposition exit.

source: Xu and Munoz-Avila (2025) Online Learning of HTN Methods for integrated LLM-HTN Planning
finding: Learning a general method from each successful LLM decomposition cuts later LLM calls and keeps or raises success.
numbers: Two domains (logistics, search and rescue), 10 random problems each, one method removed at a time; setup cost over 300 USD. Calls to ChatGPT lower with learner; success equal or higher.
limits: Small (10 problems). Learned methods are only linear lists of primitive tasks, no compound subtasks. Neither setup reaches 100%.
agent_relevance: Method library should grow from verified decompositions. Matches O3 plus library update.

source: Xu and Munoz-Avila (2025) Online Learning of HTN Methods
finding: Repeated queries without learning raise cumulative exposure to LLM errors, so success is often lower without the learner.
numbers: Authors state success is frequently lower without the learner.
limits: Qualitative explanation, not isolated by an experiment.
agent_relevance: Reusing a verified decomposition beats re-asking the model.

source: Xu and Munoz-Avila (2025) Online Learning of HTN Methods
finding: When the highest-level method is missing, success drops sharply, because the LLM must write the whole primitive sequence at once.
numbers: Low success when removing TPM2 (logistics) and SAR2 (search and rescue), Figures 8 and 9.
limits: Exact percentages only in figures.
agent_relevance: Top-level structure is the most valuable part of a method library; do not leave it to the model to improvise.

source: Prasad et al. (2023/2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
finding: Decompose only when the executor fails, recursively. This beats ReAct, plan-and-execute, Try Again and Reflexion on three agent benchmarks.
numbers: GPT-3.5. ALFWorld (dmax 3): ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Try Again 47.8, Reflexion 57.5, ADaPT 71.6. WebShop: ReAct 32, Plan-and-Execute 17, Reflexion 35, LATS 38, ADaPT 44. TextCraft (dmax 4): ReAct 19, Plan-and-Execute 27, Reflexion 32, ADaPT 52.
limits: Single runs, GPT-3.5 for main table. Pick2 in ALFWorld is 5.9 to 11.8 for most baselines (ADaPT 52.9).
agent_relevance: Support for decomposing on failure rather than upfront (an O3 trigger). Upfront plan-and-execute can be worse than no planning (WebShop 17 vs 32).

source: Prasad et al. ADaPT
finding: Needed decomposition depth grows with task complexity. ADaPT helps most where the base executor fails most.
numbers: TextCraft recipe depth 2: ReAct 26.9 vs ADaPT 78.2 (mean depth used 1.9). Depth 3: 1.8 vs 38.7 (depth used 2.8). Weak executor setting 3.3 to 41.7.
limits: Synthetic crafting tasks built to be decomposable.
agent_relevance: Depth cap should scale with task; a fixed shallow cap fails on deeper recipes.

source: Prasad et al. ADaPT
finding: Gains hold across model sizes and mixed planner/executor pairs; a strong planner can help a weak executor.
numbers: TextCraft: GPT-4 improved by up to 37 points, LLaMA by up to 15. ALFWorld dev: GPT-3.5 executor alone 38.4, GPT-3.5 planner plus executor 58.3; LLaMA-2-70B executor alone 20.4, with GPT-3.5 planner 43.3. Authors say gain is not from more LLM calls (Figure 7).
limits: Dev split; one environment for the planner-executor test.
agent_relevance: Planning with a stronger model and executing with a cheaper one is a viable split.

source: Zhou et al. (2022/2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Decompose into subproblems and solve them in order, reusing earlier answers. Huge gain on length generalisation.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: standard 16.7, chain-of-thought 16.2, least-to-most 99.7. text-davinci-002 (100 commands): 6.0, 0.0, 76.0. code-davinci-001: 0.4, 0.0, 60.7. Only 13 failures on the test set.
limits: Decomposition prompts use hand-written examples tailored to SCAN. Does not show models find decompositions unaided.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for a given decomposition scheme. The decomposition itself must be taught.

source: Zhou et al. Least-to-Most Prompting
finding: On last-letter concatenation, least-to-most is far better on long inputs and is data-efficient.
numbers: L=12: least-to-most 74.0 vs chain-of-thought 38.4 (2-shot least-to-most beat 8-shot chain-of-thought).
limits: Toy symbolic task.
agent_relevance: Decomposition pays most where length exceeds the examples.

source: Zhou et al. Least-to-Most Prompting
finding: On natural math word problems the gain is small. Failures are mostly decomposition quality.
numbers: GSM8K: chain-of-thought 60.97 to least-to-most 62.39 overall. Problems needing 5 or more steps: 39.07 to 45.23. DROP: large margin (exact figures in paper).
limits: Authors note almost every GSM8K miss is solved with a manual decomposition, so the weak link is making the decomposition.
agent_relevance: Boundary: when problems do not decompose cleanly, a decomposition step adds little.

source: Khot et al. (2022/2023) Decomposed Prompting: A Modular Approach for Solving Complex Tasks
finding: Hand-written task-specific sub-task prompts (a method library of prompts) beat one chain-of-thought prompt, also on longer inputs.
numbers: K-th letter concatenation, 100 examples per set: DecomP stays near 100% as word count grows, chain-of-thought drops. CommaQA-E: DecomP above CoT for every prompt and on the compositional split. Open-domain QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue): beats no-decomposition baseline in all settings except Codex on HotpotQA.
limits: Sub-task prompts are written by hand; each new task needs a new library. Open-domain gains are smaller than synthetic ones.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to HTN methods: a named sub-task with its own prompt and recursion.

source: Khot et al. Decomposed Prompting
finding: Finer decomposition helps a little; error analysis shows remaining errors are in sub-task answers.
numbers: CommaQA: fine-grained marginally above coarse-grained. Appendix F.2: all analysed errors were single-hop sub-question mistakes.
limits: Qualitative error sample.
agent_relevance: Verify leaf outputs; the hierarchy is rarely the failure.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2022) PlanBench
finding: Without a method library, LLMs plan poorly even on small Blocksworld, and much worse when names are obfuscated.
numbers: Plan generation Blocksworld: GPT-4 206/600 (34.3%), Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%). Mystery Blocksworld deceptive: GPT-4 26/600 (4.3%), Instruct-GPT3 14/600 (0.23%); randomized: 12/600 (2%) and 6/600 (1%).
limits: Plain classical planning, no HTN decomposition. Prompt style fixed.
agent_relevance: Looks like pattern matching, not planning. Lower baseline that decomposition by known methods must beat.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Cannot Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Autonomous LLM planning is weak. Use the LLM as a generator with external verifying critics in a loop.
numbers: On average only about 12% of plans from GPT-4 are executable and reach the goal.
quote: only about 12% of the plans that the best LLM (GPT-4) generates are actually executable
limits: Position paper reusing earlier results. Not a new controlled test.
agent_relevance: Supports a generate-then-verify loop around decomposition.

source: Xie et al. (2024) TravelPlanner
finding: Long multi-constraint planning is almost unsolved by LLM agents even with tools.
numbers: 1,225 queries. Best: GPT-4-Turbo with ReAct final pass rate 0.6% in two-stage mode; other LLMs passed none.
limits: Different task type from HTN; constraint-heavy.
agent_relevance: Shows the ceiling of flat prompting on large plans; decomposition and constraint checks are the missing parts.

source: Puerta-Merino et al. (2025) A Roadmap to Guide the Integration of LLMs in Hierarchical Planning
finding: A plain LLM planner on IPC-2023 total-order HTN problems almost never produces a correct plan, and none with correct decomposition.
numbers: Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B: 3% correct plans, 0% correct hierarchical decomposition. Upper bound PandaDealer-agile-lama (IPC-2023 total-order satisficing winner). Benchmark has 22 domains.
limits: Preliminary work; one baseline LLM.
agent_relevance: Raw LLMs do not decompose by method on their own. A given method library is needed.

source: Meneguzzi et al. (2026) Hierarchical Task Network Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics
finding: LLM-written search heuristics for HTN planning nearly match the best HTN planner in coverage and expand far fewer nodes.
numbers: Six total-order domains, 139 problems, nine LLMs, 780 candidate heuristics. LLM virtual best solves 131/139; PANDA RCFF 134, LMCOUNT 118, TDG 117, PANDA RCLMCut 113. On 125 shared problems the LLM expands fewer nodes on 104 (83%).
limits: Virtual-best over algorithms and models. Planner is PYTRICH.
agent_relevance: The decomposition space still needs search guidance; the model can propose it, a loop must test it.

source: Meneguzzi et al. (2026) HTN Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics
finding: Most generated heuristic code fails, and which model you use matters more than which search algorithm.
numbers: Of 780 candidates, 419 passed local selection, 347 viable, 72 broke on every problem (60 of 72 assumed a wrong state type). Best-to-worst gap among five main models is about 27 times in median node expansions. Four models (GPT-4o, Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, GPT-5.2) had no surviving candidate in five of six domains.
limits: Failures persisted despite explicit interface in the prompt. No prompt retries.
agent_relevance: Generate many, filter by execution, keep survivors. Expect large model variance.

source: Why Do LLM-based Web Agents Fail? A Hierarchical Planning Perspective (2026)
finding: On web tasks, high-level plans are not the main bottleneck. Execution of each step is. Structured PDDL plans align better with human subgoals than natural-language plans.
numbers: Perfect matches 67.7% (PDDL) vs 60.6% (NL); unmatched 15.4% vs 29.4%. Executor gpt-5-nano: 38.5% plan completion, 36.4% final success. With human plans claude-haiku-4.5 29.2%, gemini-flash-2.5 17.3%.
limits: Web domain; alignment judged with an LLM, so scoring noise possible.
agent_relevance: Decomposition quality can be good while step execution fails. Spend checks at the leaf level.

source: Meneguzzi et al. (2026), reporting the IPC 2020 HTN track
finding: Domain-independent HTN heuristics have not clearly beaten plain recursive search: the IPC-2020 HTN winner used efficient recursion and bookkeeping, not a heuristic.
numbers: IPC-2020 winner HYPERTENSION. Number of competing planners not recorded.
limits: Secondhand statement from a 2026 paper.
agent_relevance: The method library itself, not clever search, carries the performance.
